rationale: The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 places the memory patches anterior to the scene perception areas, while Option 2 places them posterior. The paper proposes a convergence zone for scene perception and visuospatial memory at the edge of high-level visual cortex. Anterior placement, which lies beyond the perceptual areas, fits a memory-driven region that interfaces with perception while staying separated from it, consistent with the paper's framing of avoiding sensory-mnemonic interference. Posterior placement would sit within the perceptual hierarchy, weakening that separation. So Option 1 is somewhat better news for the proposed account.

The two abstracts differ only in whether the memory-responsive patches lie posterior (Option 1) or anterior (Option 2) to the scene perception areas. The paper proposes a convergence zone at the posterior edge of high-level visual cortex, interfacing sensory and mnemonic representations while avoiding interference. A posterior location fits the proposed account of adjacent yet distinct sensory and memory regions, so Option 1 supports the paper's hypothesis more directly.

The paper proposes that the Pdyn+ CeA-to-PBN pathway regulates itch, with the central claim that it inhibits itch signaling. Option 1 reports suppression of scratching, reduced PBN Fos, and raised pain thresholds, all consistent with an inhibitory itch-regulating pathway, which supports the paper's hypothesis. Option 2 reports the opposite on every measure (enhanced scratching, increased Fos, lowered thresholds), which would contradict an inhibitory role. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that the Pdyn+ CeA-to-PBN pathway regulates itch. Option 1 reports that stimulating this pathway increases scratching, enhances PBN Fos, and lowers pain thresholds, which supports a pro-itch, pro-nociceptive role for the pathway as hypothesized. Option 2 reports the opposite: stimulation inhibits scratching, suppresses PBN Fos, and raises thresholds. Option 2 would argue against the pathway promoting itch, so Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper's proposed account is that endothelial cells are regionally heterogeneous and that AD endothelial cells show upregulated protein folding genes with distinct responses to plaques and CAA. Option 1 reports exactly these findings (regional heterogeneity, upregulated protein folding, distinct responses), so it supports the paper's thesis. Option 2 reports homogeneity, downregulated folding, and similar responses, which undercut the proposed account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper's proposed account is that endothelial cells show regional homogeneity and that AD endothelial cells have downregulated protein folding genes, with similar responses to plaques and CAA. Option 1 matches this account (homogeneity, downregulated protein folding). Option 2 reports heterogeneity and upregulated protein folding, which contradicts the paper's central framing. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper defends the view that hippocampal theta is a key memory modulator and that narrowband theta reflects memory. Option 1 reports narrowband 3-4 Hz theta increasing during encoding and before recall, which supports the proposed theta-memory account and the masking explanation. Option 2 reverses these effects, contradicting the paper's central claim that theta supports memory. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that hippocampal theta is a key modulator of memory, consistent with computational models, and that narrowband theta masked by broadband effects is the relevant signal. Option 2 reports theta increases during encoding and recall, directly supporting the theta-memory account the paper defends. Option 1 reports theta decreases, which contradicts the stated models and the paper's own framing of theta as memory-relevant. Thus Option 2 is clearly better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that motion cues alone can drive robust object category responses across visual cortex. Option 1 reports that posterior ventral regions decode better with static images, while anterior and dorsal regions decode better with dynamic kinematograms. Option 2 reverses this, saying posterior ventral regions favor dynamic stimuli. Option 1's pattern fits the traditional view that ventral cortex is form-driven, which the paper's framing emphasizes as a surprise to overcome. Option 2's pattern, with posterior ventral regions favoring motion, would strengthen the claim that motion supports category coding even in ventral cortex, which is the paper's main thesis. So Option 2 is the better news for the paper's motion-based account.

The paper proposes that motion cues alone can drive robust object category responses. Option 1 reports posterior occipitotemporal and ventral regions decoding better for dynamic stimuli and anterior/dorsal for static, which fits a motion-as-category-cue account in ventral cortex (the paper's emphasis on dynamic luminance cues matching). Option 2 reverses the regional pattern, placing the dynamic advantage in anterior/dorsal regions, which is less consistent with the narrative that motion supports ventral category processing. Option 1 is modestly better news for the proposed account.

Both abstracts are identical except for which sex shows the PrL-DT relationship and drug-seeking link. Option 1 attributes the proposed PrL mechanism and its link to drug-seeking to males; Option 2 attributes it to females. The paper's proposed account is that PrL activity underlies distress tolerance and predicts drug-seeking. Option 1 supports this account in the sex the paper emphasizes, while Option 2 does too but for females. Since the hypothesis itself (PrL role in DT and drug-seeking) is supported equally in both, the difference is mainly which sex is highlighted, so the news value is near neutral, with a slight edge to Option 1 for the sexes' distinct effects being framed as a clean male finding.

Both options describe the same study design and hypothesis: PrL activity underlies distress tolerance and links to drug-seeking. The only difference is which sex shows the effects (females in Option 1, males in Option 2). The paper's proposed account is that PrL-mediated DT predicts drug-seeking, and both versions support this equally. Option 1 supports the account with the sex that the framing emphasizes as the novel finding (females, a historically understudied group), but the core mechanistic claim is equivalent in both, so the difference is roughly neutral for the proposed hypothesis.

The two abstracts are identical except for which brain region is linked to mean control versus covariance control. The paper proposes a stochastic control framework that decomposes control cost into mean and covariance components. Option 1 reports lower visual areas controlling means and PCC controlling covariances; Option 2 reverses this. Neither result clearly favors the framework itself, since the framework's utility is shown either way. The difference is only which region is assigned to which component, so it is roughly neutral for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes a linear stochastic framework for control costs decomposed into mean and covariance components. The two options differ only in which brain region (lower visual areas vs posterior cingulate cortex) is associated with controlling means versus covariances. Option 1 assigns covariance control to visual areas and mean control to PCC; Option 2 reverses this. Neither clearly supports the framework more than the other; the difference concerns which regional attribution is reported, which is essentially neutral for the method's validity, though a near-even split is most appropriate.

The paper proposes that age-related differences in fluid intelligence are partly mediated by frontoparietal responsiveness to cognitive demand. Option 1 says mediation is specifically associated with voxels most activated by cognitive demand, which directly supports the proposed frontoparietal activation account. Option 2 says mediation is associated with voxels suppressed by demand and not activated ones, which undercuts the activation-based mechanism the paper defends. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis. The physical-activity moderation details are exploratory and secondary.

Both abstracts share the core model: frontoparietal responsiveness mediates age-related fluid intelligence decline. They differ in which voxels mediate (suppressed vs activated by demand) and in which activity dimension moderates (frequency vs variety). The paper's central proposed mechanism is frontoparietal responsiveness to novel problem-solving, and Option 1 localizes mediation to deactivated (suppressed) voxels, a more specific and somewhat surprising finding, while Option 2 localizes it to activated voxels, the more expected account consistent with the introduction's framing. Option 2 aligns more directly with the prior literature the paper builds on, so it is slightly better news for the proposed account.

The paper proposes that danger shifts consolidation from PRh toward BLA, with initial pairings encoded in BLA and later pairings in PRh, plus mutual inhibition between regions. Option 1 matches this account exactly. Option 2 reverses the regional assignments (BLA to PRh shift, PRh encoding initial pairings), contradicting the proposed model. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's hypothesis better.

Both abstracts share the same framing and hypothesis: danger shifts consolidation between PRh and BLA via mutually inhibitory interactions. The paper's proposed account is that danger shifts consolidation of the S2-S1 association to the PRh (Option 1) versus to the BLA (Option 2), and that initial pairings are encoded in PRh vs BLA respectively. Option 1 matches the paper's stated mechanism more directly, with the mutual inhibition story and the PRh-consolidation outcome under danger. Option 2 reverses the region assignments, which would contradict the proposed account of PRh-driven recognition memory. So Option 1 is better news for the paper's proposed account.

Both abstracts describe the same design and the same lateral-to-medial partition development, but Option 1 reports faster lateral thalamus development, linear increases in fiber integrity, and frontal connections developing later, while Option 2 reports reduction, decrease, earlier frontal development, and slower lateral development. The paper's proposed account is a posterior-to-anterior developmental gradient of thalamocortical connectivity. Option 1's frontal-later finding is consistent with a posterior-to-anterior gradient, whereas Option 2's frontal-earlier finding contradicts it. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's account better.

Both abstracts share the same framing and hypothesis: thalamic development is characterized by a lateral-to-medial partition pattern and a developmental gradient of thalamocortical connectivity. Option 1 reports medial shrinkage, lateral-slower development, and frontal connections developing earlier (a posterior-to-anterior gradient consistent with the paper's conclusion). Option 2 reports lateral expansion, faster lateral development, and frontal connections developing later, which contradicts the stated posterior-to-anterior gradient. The gradient claim in Option 1 is internally consistent with its findings, so Option 1 better supports the paper's proposed account.

Both options share the same background and framing. Option 1 reports that silencing cortico-thalamic feedback reduces state-dependent differences in dLGN responses to visual stimuli for both temporal and spatial features, supporting the paper's claim that feedback drives the state-dependent shift. Option 2 reports that silencing feedback increases these differences, and oddly mentions auditory stimuli and a 'late stage', which is internally inconsistent with the visual framing and undermines the proposed account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper argues that cortico-thalamic feedback drives state-dependent modulation of dLGN visual responses. Option 2 supports this claim (silencing feedback reduces state differences, for both temporal and spatial features), whereas Option 1 reports that silencing feedback increases state differences, which would undercut the feedback-dependence account. Option 2 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

Both options share the same framework: ON/OFF pathway dominance shifting with contrast. The paper's proposed account is that high-contrast stimuli favor OFF dominance and low-contrast favor ON dominance, with ON pathways more contrast-sensitive. Option 1 matches this account exactly, including the predicted loss of low-contrast vision with ON deficits, so it supports the paper's hypothesis more strongly than Option 2, which reverses the contrast-polarity relationship and conflicts with the stated higher ON contrast sensitivity.

Both options share the same core claim: ON and OFF pathways separately process light and dark stimuli, with contrast shifting dominance. The paper's proposed account is that low contrast favors OFF dominance and high contrast favors ON dominance, consistent with ON pathways being less contrast-sensitive. Option 1 matches this account exactly, with its predicted deficit being OFF-pathway loss. Option 2 reverses the contrast-dominance mapping, which contradicts the stated lower/higher contrast sensitivity rationale, so it is weaker support for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same core claim: endogenous rhythms in eye movements cohere with EEG oscillations, supporting linguistic processing imposing time scales. They differ only in the topography: Option 1 places theta over the whole head and delta over occipital sites, while Option 2 reverses this. The paper's proposed account rests on frequency-selective coherence in general, which holds equally in both; the spatial assignment is a secondary detail that neither clearly strengthens nor weakens the endogenous-rhythm hypothesis, though a whole-head delta effect linked to sentence-level chunking could be marginally more consistent with a linguistic (non-visual) origin. Overall the difference is close to neutral for the proposed account.

The two abstracts differ only in the topography and band pairings: Option 1 links saccade rhythms to occipital theta and fixation rhythms to whole-head delta; Option 2 swaps these to whole-head theta and occipital delta. The paper's proposed account is that linguistic processing imposes endogenous rhythms on reading. Option 1's pairing of word-level saccades with occipital (visual) activity and sentence-level fixation rhythms with whole-head activity fits more naturally with a visual-sampling and higher-level chunking story, though the difference is modest and both preserve the core claim.

The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 attributes the abstraction benefit and the distinct neural responses to REM cueing, while Option 2 attributes them to SWS cueing. The paper's proposed account is that targeted memory reactivation during sleep facilitates visual rule abstraction, with a delayed effect. Option 1 supports a REM-specific mechanism, Option 2 an SWS-specific one. Neither is clearly favored by the framing, so the difference is roughly neutral with respect to the paper's core claim, though the paper's stated hypothesis is about reactivation in sleep generally.

The two abstracts are identical except that Option 1 reports the abstraction benefit and neural responses for SWS cueing, while Option 2 reports them for REM cueing. The paper proposes that targeted memory reactivation during sleep facilitates visual rule abstraction, with SWS as the favored stage given the framing of SWS-linked plasticity. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's central account more directly, making it better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that VTA dopamine neurons provide motivational value to actions and cues (critic-like role, flexible persistent pursuit) while SNc neurons support precise, action-specific learning (actor-like role). Option 1 assigns these functions as the paper's framework states. Option 2 swaps VTA and SNc roles, which contradicts the proposed separable-systems architecture and the stated actor-critic mapping. Thus Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts are identical except for swapping which dopamine population is assigned to motivational value (flexible pursuit) versus time-limited precise learning. Option 1 assigns motivational/flexible function to SNc and precise learning to VTA, with SNc instructing the critic and VTA the actor. Option 2 reverses these. The paper's proposed architecture is the separable actor-critic division with heterogeneous dopamine systems; which population gets which role determines whether the proposed account is supported as stated. Option 1 aligns with the conventional view of VTA as the motivational/critic-like system and SNc as action-specific, so the claim as worded in Option 1 is less surprising but the paper's core claim of separable processes holds in both. Overall the difference is a reassignment of roles, so it is only modestly good or bad news for the paper's own account, leaning slightly toward Option 1 being the more coherent framing of the proposed actor-critic mapping.

The two abstracts differ only in the sign of the pupil-neural/blood correlations and the direction of blink effects. Option 1 reports negative correlations during rest and NREM, positive during alertness and REM, and blinks increasing arousal and decreasing blood volume in sleep. Option 2 reports the reverse signs throughout. The paper's proposed account is that arousal strongly couples pupil size to cerebrovascular and neural dynamics in a state-dependent way. Option 1's pattern of state-dependent sign reversal with blinks linked to arousal is coherent with that account and with known pupil-arousal and sleep-hemodynamic relationships, so it reads as somewhat better support for the paper's view.

The two abstracts differ only in the signs of the pupil-neural/vascular correlations and the blink effect. Option 1 reports positive correlations during rest and NREM and blinking associated with decreased arousal and increased blood volume during sleep, consistent with the paper's framing that arousal drives coupled neural and vascular dynamics (pupil tracks gamma and blood volume). Option 2 reverses these signs, which would undercut the claimed coupling pattern and the blink-related arousal account. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed account better.

Both abstracts describe the same study on apical cochlear tonotopy. Option 1 reports that responses differ across the apex in a pattern consistent with the base, supporting the paper's view that a common tonotopic organization extends to the apex. Option 2 reports no differences in a pattern inconsistent with the base, which is a double negative that effectively says the apex does not follow the base-like pattern, undermining the paper's proposed account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's position.

The paper proposes that tonotopic organization extends to the cochlear apex in low-frequency animals, consistent with the base-of-cochlea pattern established by von Békésy and later work. Option 2 reports responses differing across the apex in a pattern consistent with the base, supporting the paper's account of an orderly tonotopic map. Option 1 reports no such difference, which would undermine the proposed tonotopic account. Option 2 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's position.

Both abstracts share the same core claim: respiration dynamically entrains prefrontal activity depending on behavioral state. The only difference is which state shows stronger gamma entrainment (HC in Option 1, TS in Option 2) and which shows superficial-layer recruitment. Option 1 has gamma entrainment strongest in home cage, which is the baseline/resting state and a plausible, unsurprising finding for a respiration-coupling account; Option 2 frames tail-suspension stress as the state of strongest gamma entrainment, a more striking stress-linked result that could support a state-dependent stress-engagement narrative. Neither clearly strengthens the paper's central claim more than the other, so the difference is roughly neutral, with a slight tilt toward Option 2 for a more interesting state-dependent framing.

The two abstracts differ only in which state shows stronger gamma entrainment by respiration (TS in Option 1, HC in Option 2) and which state recruits superficial versus deep layers. The paper's proposed account is that respiration dynamically entrains prefrontal activity depending on behavioral state, with stress-related passive coping being a focal condition. Option 1 frames the stressful TS state as having the strongest respiratory entrainment of gamma, which supports a state-dependent, stress-sensitive respiration-coupling account more directly than Option 2, where HC dominates. The layer findings are secondary. Overall Option 1 is modestly better news for the paper's proposed dynamic-entrainment account.

The paper proposes that otitis media-related auditory deprivation alters the descending olivocochlear efferent system and that this relates to poorer speech-in-noise recognition. Option 1 reports weaker efferent inhibition and worse performance (higher SNR needed), which fits the proposed impaired central auditory processing account. Option 2 reports stronger inhibition and better performance, which would undercut the deprivation-impairment hypothesis the paper defends.

The paper proposes that otitis media-related auditory deprivation alters the descending olivocochlear efferent system, impairing speech-in-noise recognition. Option 1 reports stronger efferent inhibition and lower SNR thresholds (better performance) in the otitis media group; Option 2 reports weaker inhibition and higher SNR needed (worse performance). Option 2 aligns with the paper's hypothesis of impaired central auditory processing linked to efferent changes, so Option 1 is worse news for the proposed account.

The paper proposes that hV6A sends signals to M1 via a short parieto-frontal route during reach planning. Option 1 reports inhibition of MEPs by hV6A, Option 2 reports facilitation. For a hypothesis that the parieto-frontal pathway actively contributes to reach planning, a clear, interpretable directional effect (facilitation, consistent with excitatory drive toward motor output) is typically read as more supportive of an active functional connection than inhibition, which is harder to link to a planning role. Both options support the core claim of an active short route, so the difference is moderately favorable to Option 2.

The paper proposes that hV6A sends signals to M1 via a short parieto-frontal route during reach planning. Option 1 reports facilitation of motor-evoked potentials, consistent with excitatory flow that supports the proposed pathway being active and transmitting reach-relevant information. Option 2 reports inhibition, which would suggest a different, suppressive influence and undercut the claim of an excitatory parieto-frontal route. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's account.

The paper proposes that corticofugal activity engages intracollicular inhibitory circuits via recurrent excitation of GABA neurons, explaining the net inhibition seen in physiology. Option 1 supports this account directly: descending signals drive GABA neurons and generate local inhibition. Option 2 reverses the circuit logic, claiming recurrent inhibition drives glutamatergic neurons and produces local excitation, which contradicts the paper's central thesis about corticofugal inhibition. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that corticofugal signals engage intracollicular excitatory circuits via recurrent inhibition of GABA neurons, dampening corticofugal activity and driving glutamatergic IC neurons. Option 1 matches this mechanism: tonically firing glutamatergic neurons are excited, GABA neurons fire during repetitive activity, and polysynaptic inhibition of glutamatergic neurons generates local excitation. Option 2 reverses the cell types, making glutamatergic neurons the GABA-driven targets and yielding local inhibition, which contradicts the paper's proposed account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes an internal model for vibrissa positioning. Option 1 finds peripheral reafference is not required and motor cortex is needed only without reafference, supporting a flexible internal model that works through either mechanism. Option 2 finds both reafference and motor cortex are required, which implies a model that depends on external feedback and cortex together. The internal-model account the paper defends is more sharply supported by Option 1's dissociable, redundant mechanisms, since it explains the results without requiring every component; Option 2 is a more restrictive, less parsimonious conclusion that the paper's framing ('requires either') would not match.

The paper proposes an internal model for vibrissa positioning relying on peripheral reafference and motor cortex. Option 1 reports that peripheral reafference is required and motor cortex is required alongside it, supporting a model where both are necessary, which strengthens the paper's proposed account of a feedback-dependent internal model. Option 2 reports neither is required, weakening the claim that these mechanisms are needed and making the proposed account less compelling. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that a global rise of inhibition (from FSNs) drives initiation and execution of spontaneous motor actions. Option 1 supports this directly: FSNs fire longer and earlier, carry more movement-onset information, show stereotyped responses, and silencing FSNs reduces licking. Option 2 reverses these findings, attributing the drive to excitation from PNs, which contradicts the paper's proposed account. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper's proposed account is that a global rise of excitation (from pyramidal neurons carrying most movement-onset information and driving licking) contributes to initiating and executing spontaneous movements. Option 1 supports this excitation-centered account, with PNs carrying more information and silencing PNs reducing licking. Option 2 instead attributes the account to inhibition, which contradicts the paper's defended mechanism. Thus Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in swapping which measure (CT or SA) shows the anterior-posterior genetic division and which shows within-lobe proximity, and which measure shows the strongest neonate-adult similarity in the medial surface. The paper's central proposal is that CT and SA have spatially distinct genetic topographies in neonates. Option 1 assigns the anterior-posterior pattern to CT and the within-lobe pattern to SA, which matches the known contrast that CT tends to follow anterior-posterior (regional/gradient) organization while SA is more lobar. Option 1 also attributes medial-surface neonate-adult similarity to SA, which fits the structural-genetic picture the paper defends. Option 2 reverses these assignments, which would be less consistent with the proposed framework, so Option 1 is somewhat better news.

The two abstracts differ only in swapping which measure (CT or SA) shows the anterior-posterior division versus the within-lobe pattern, and which measure shows the strongest neonate-adult similarity in the medial surface. The paper's proposed account is that CT and SA have distinct genetic topographies established in the neonatal brain. Option 1 matches the prior adult literature's pattern that SA is more anterior-posterior organized and CT more lobe-organized, and places the medial CT similarity, which is consistent with the paper's framing of differential genetic regulation. Option 2 reverses these assignments, which is less coherent with the stated hypothesis of differential CT/SA genetic patterning, so Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ only in which neuron type shows greater Ca2+ influx, vesicle coupling, compact active zone organization, and Ca2+ channel stoichiometry. The paper's proposed account is that nano-architecture and Ca2+ influx together tune release differently in tonic versus phasic synapses. Option 1 assigns the enhanced Ca2+ influx and compact organization to phasic release sites, which fits a mechanism explaining phasic synapses' distinctive release. Option 2 assigns them to tonic sites, which would instead support the mechanism for tonic synapses. Either option supports a differential-tuning account, but the direction of the specific features is the only difference, so Option 1 is modestly better news for the paper's framing of phasic-site specialization.

The two abstracts differ only in which neuron type shows greater Ca2+ influx and compact active zone organization: Option 1 assigns these to tonic release sites, Option 2 to phasic. The paper's proposed account is that nano-architecture and Ca2+ influx together tune release differently across tonic and phasic subtypes; both versions support that account equally. The directional difference is a matter of which subtype is favored, not a clear gain or loss for the central hypothesis, so the news value for the paper's proposed account is roughly neutral, with Option 1 marginally aligning with the expected pattern of tonic synapses having more compact, Ca-channel-enriched sites.

The two abstracts are identical except for one detail: where Sema5A/5B are expressed, medulla (Option 1) versus pons (Option 2). The paper proposes that Sema5A/5B-PlexA1/A3 signaling inhibits premature defasciculation of CS axons at the decussation site. Anatomically, the decussation of CS axons occurs in the medulla (pyramidal decussation), so expression at the medulla is consistent with the proposed mechanism and supports it more directly. Expression in the pons would be less consistent with the decussation site, weakening the paper's account. Therefore Option 1 is better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The two abstracts are identical except Option 1 places Sema5A/5B expression in the pons at the decussation site, while Option 2 places it in the medulla. The paper's proposed account is that Sema5A/5B-PlexA1/A3 signaling inhibits premature defasciculation of CS axons at the decussation site. Anatomically, the pyramidal decussation occurs in the caudal medulla, so Option 2's medullary localization is more consistent with the claimed mechanism, making Option 2 marginally better support for the paper's account. The difference is small and mainly about anatomical precision.

The two abstracts are identical except Option 1 reports a significant prolonged alkalization at the cholinergic NMJ, while Option 2 reports a reduction of alkalization at a glutamatergic synapse. The paper's proposed account is that cleft alkalization from postsynaptic Ca2+ and PMCA drives pH transients. Option 1 supports this account more directly, since it shows alkalization as the typical response, whereas Option 2 weakens it by reporting diminished alkalization. Option 2 also mislabels the NMJ as glutamatergic, which is a factual error. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed mechanism.

Both abstracts propose the same hypothesis: NMJ cleft alkalization driven by postsynaptic Ca2+ and PMCA, with acidification under strenuous stimulation. The key difference is Option 1 reports a 'significant reduction of alkalization' at 5 s stimulation, while Option 2 reports a 'significant and prolonged alkalization.' Option 2's result more directly supports the paper's proposed mechanism of activity-induced alkalization via muscle Ca2+ extrusion, so Option 1 is worse news for the paper's account.

The paper proposes that NMDA receptors mediate activity-dependent alignment of L5-V1 inputs in the SC. Option 1 reports the NMDA receptor knockout disrupting L5-V1 terminal organization, which directly supports the paper's account. Option 2 reports the same finding for AMPA receptors, which would not support the paper's NMDA-centered hypothesis and is therefore weaker news for it. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposal.

The paper's hypothesis is that activity-dependent glutamate receptor signaling mediates visual map alignment in the SC. Option 1 reports AMPA receptor knockout disrupting L5-V1 terminal organization with retinocollicular topography unaffected, supporting a role for AMPA receptors. Option 2 reports the same pattern for NMDA receptors. Both are equally supportive of the paper's central account (receptor-mediated activity-dependent alignment), so the choice between them is roughly neutral for the proposed mechanism, with the study's framing of AMPA receptors as the mediator in Option 1 being comparable to NMDA in Option 2.

The two abstracts differ only in how MFN2 is perturbed: Option 1 uses knockdown, Option 2 uses overexpression. The paper's proposed account is that fusion-related QC supports presynaptic Ca2+ handling and the SV cycle. Both versions report the same qualitative pattern, but knockdown is the loss-of-function manipulation that cleanly tests whether MFN2-dependent fusion is required for QC. Overexpression is a gain-of-function manipulation that can confound interpretation, so reporting it as the source of the same effects is weaker support for the fusion-based QC account. Option 1 therefore modestly favors the paper's thesis.

The two abstracts differ only in whether MFN2 was overexpressed (Option 1) or knocked down (Option 2). Both report the same qualitative outcomes: reduced trafficking and fusion, decreased SV proteins, inhibited exocytosis, Ca2+ dyshomeostasis, and enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ sequestration. The paper's proposed account is an active fusion-related QC process supporting presynaptic Ca2+ handling and the SV cycle. Since the reported effects are the same in direction under either manipulation, the choice of overexpression versus knockdown does not clearly favor the paper's hypothesis either way.

The paper proposes that α9k1 integrin signaling drives CNS sensory regeneration via a distinctive program. Option 1 reports the CNS program shows little correlation with embryonic or PNS programs, supporting the claim that it is distinctive and not a recapitulation of developmental or PNS regeneration. Option 2 reports high correlation, undermining the 'distinctive program' claim. Thus Option 1 is better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ only in whether the CNS regeneration program shows high correlation with embryonic development or PNS regeneration (Option 1) or little correlation (Option 2). The paper's proposed account is that CNS regeneration engages a distinctive program that differs from PNS regeneration. Option 2's 'little correlation' directly supports this distinctiveness claim, while Option 1's high correlation weakens it. So Option 1 is worse news for the paper's central account.

The paper proposes that hallucination proneness reflects direct alterations in perceptual priors independent of sensory noise. Option 1 reports a circumscribed prior bias unrelated to sensory noise and sensory resolution, directly supporting that account. Option 2 reports a general prior bias tied to sensory noise and sensory resolution, which supports the indirect, sensory-driven alternative the paper argues against. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that hallucination proneness reflects indirect alterations in perceptual priors dependent on sensory noise. Option 1 reports a general prior bias related to sensory noise and sensory resolution, supporting the indirect, noise-dependent account. Option 2 reports a circumscribed bias unrelated to sensory noise, supporting a direct prior-alteration account, which contradicts the paper's proposed mechanism. Thus Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's defended hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in the final key claim. Option 1 says intracellular structures are shared between assemblies, entangling them into larger complexes or association domains, which supports the paper's proposed model of coordinated, combined transsynaptic assemblies resembling nanocolumns. Option 2 reverses this to disintegrating assemblies into smaller complexes or segregation domains, which undermines the paper's argument that assemblies combine into functional units and physically connect compartments. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The two abstracts differ only in wording: Option 1 says assemblies 'disintegrate' into smaller complexes or 'segregation domains' with intercellular structures shared, while Option 2 says intracellular structures are shared and 'entangle' them into 'larger complexes' or 'association domains'. The paper's proposed account is that transsynaptic assemblies physically link the three compartments and organize into functional domains resembling nanocolumns. Option 2's larger, entangled complexes and association domains fit that connected-organization account better than Option 1's disintegration into smaller segregated units, so Option 1 is somewhat worse news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that GluA1 ubiquitination at K868 is needed for proper bidirectional plasticity and cognition. Option 1 reports enhanced LTP with LTD deficits; Option 2 reports the reverse. Both report cognitive deficits. The proposed account is that ubiquitination regulates AMPAR stability and thus bidirectional plasticity; blocking it (K868R) should disrupt that balance in either direction, so the direction of the LTP/LTD change is not clearly favoring one. Option 1's LTP enhancement with LTD deficit is a somewhat less intuitive reading of loss of degradation-driven AMPAR turnover, but both are consistent with a disrupted bidirectional system, making the difference modest.

The paper proposes that GluA1 ubiquitination at K868 is physiologically important for bidirectional plasticity and cognition, by controlling AMPAR degradation and synaptic stability. Option 1 reports enhanced LTD and LTP deficits, which fits a model where ubiquitination-driven receptor removal supports LTD and blocking it impairs LTP. Option 2 reverses this, showing enhanced LTP and LTD deficits, which would conflict with the proposed mechanism that ubiquitination-dependent degradation promotes depression. Both preserve the cognitive deficits, so the difference rests on which plasticity direction is affected, and Option 1 aligns better with the paper's framing of the mechanism.

The two abstracts differ in key claims. Option 1 says diffusible tau lowers the threshold for Aβ to inhibit LTP (promoting Aβ synaptotoxicity), says disruption persists for 2 weeks, and describes rapid onset. Option 2 says tau heightens the threshold (protective-seeming, opposing the paper's claim of promoting Aβ toxicity), and describes slow onset. The paper's proposed account is that diffusible tau drives rapid, persistent plasticity deficits and promotes Aβ synaptotoxicity. Option 1 matches this account strongly, while Option 2 contradicts the promotion claim and weakens the rapid-onset framing.

Both abstracts report the same core findings: patient-derived aqueous extracts inhibit LTP, tau is required with Abeta, and effects persist. The paper's proposed hypothesis is that diffusible tau drives synaptic dysfunction. Option 1 says tau heightens the threshold for Abeta (tau is protective or dampening), and describes a slow onset of tau-driven deficits. Option 2 says tau lowers the threshold for Abeta (tau sensitizes, consistent with promoting Abeta toxicity), and describes rapid onset. Option 2 aligns better with the paper's conclusion that diffusible tau promotes Abeta-mediated dysfunction and causes rapid onset deficits, so Option 1 is worse news for the proposed hypothesis.

Both abstracts propose the same hypothesis: ELS-activated neuronal ensembles are reactivated by adult stress and encode stress hypersensitivity. Option 1 reports that inhibiting ELS-activated NAc neurons ameliorates social avoidance, which supports the proposed account that these ensembles drive stress hypersensitivity. Option 2 reports the opposite direction in CA1 (exacerbated avoidance) and uses hM3Dq, a mismatch with inhibition. That result is inconsistent with the paper's proposed mechanism, so Option 1 is clearly better news for the hypothesis.

Both versions propose the same hypothesis: ELS-activated neuronal ensembles are preferentially reactivated by adult stress and encode stress hypersensitivity. The key difference is the region and the outcome of inhibition. Option 1 reports that inhibiting ELS-activated CA1 neurons exacerbates social avoidance, which supports the idea that these ensembles normally buffer stress and that their reactivation drives hypersensitivity in a protective-loss sense, making the account less straightforward. Option 2 reports that inhibiting ELS-activated NAc neurons ameliorates social avoidance, which directly supports the claim that reactivation of these ensembles causes stress hypersensitivity. Option 2 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that the ongoing local GABAergic barrage drives the irregular firing of GPe neurons. Option 1 reports that silencing PV+ neurons increases firing rate and regularity of PV- neurons, and that unitary inputs produce large increases in firing irregularity, consistent with the barrage causing irregularity. Option 2 reports the opposite: silencing decreases regularity and inhibition decreases irregularity, which contradicts the central claim that the inhibitory barrage produces irregular firing. Option 1 therefore supports the paper's proposed account better.

The paper argues that the ongoing local inhibitory barrage produces the irregular firing of GPe neurons in vivo. Option 1 shows silencing PV+ neurons decreases PV- firing rate and regularity, and dynamic clamp with inhibition reduces irregularity, supporting the barrage-as-source-of-irregularity account. Option 2 reverses these: silencing increases irregularity and inhibition increases irregularity, which contradicts the paper's proposed account that the barrage generates the irregular pattern. Option 1 therefore is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ in key results. Option 1 reports PVT activation by acute stress, dmPFC somatostatin neurons mediating suppression of PV neurons, preservation of the original memory, and PVT activity during conditioning impairing PV synaptic modification and abolishing probabilistic fear memory. Option 2 reports repetitive stress, a less specific GABA population, disruption of the original memory, and PVT activity enhancing PV synaptic modification and helping memory formation. The paper's proposed account is PVT as a stress sensor that tunes prefrontal inhibition. Option 1's results are internally coherent with that account and with a memory-preserving, reversible modulation, while Option 2's results (enhancement of formation, disruption of memory) fit a weaker or inverted version of the proposed mechanism, so Option 1 is better news for the paper's hypothesis.

Both abstracts describe the same proposed account: PVT as a stress sensor tuning dmPFC inhibitory circuits to modulate probabilistic fear memory. Option 1 reports repetitive stress activating PVT, GABA-neuron mediated suppression of PV cells, enhanced synaptic modification during conditioning that helps form the memory, and disruption of the original memory. Option 2 reports acute stress, somatostatin neurons, impaired synaptic modification that abolishes memory formation, and preservation of the memory. The paper's proposed account is that PVT-driven circuit modulation shapes memory; Option 1's findings (memory formation facilitated, memory disrupted by modulation) align more directly with a strong, mechanistic role for the stress-PVT-dmPFC pathway in altering memory, whereas Option 2's findings suggest the pathway merely preserves memory and abolishes formation, which is a somewhat weaker and less coherent demonstration of the proposed sensor role.

The paper proposes that GC GLP-1R+ neurons suppress food intake (homeostatic and hedonic) via GLP-1R agonism. Option 1 reports depolarization by exendin-4, chemogenetic stimulation reducing intake, and GC GLP-1R agonism reducing intake, all consistent with the proposed satiety role. Option 2 reports polarization (ambiguous/likely hyperpolarization, a mismatch with depolarization), and stimulation increasing intake, which contradicts the proposed account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that GC GLP-1R+ neurons act in homeostatic and hedonic food intake, consistent with GLP-1R agonism suppressing food intake elsewhere. Option 2 reports that GLP-1R agonism depolarizes these neurons and that stimulating them reduces homeostatic intake, which matches the expected anorectic role of GLP-1 signaling. Option 1 reports depolarization being suppressed (polarized, ambiguous) and that stimulation increases intake, contradicting the known GLP-1 anorectic framework and the paper's proposed role. So Option 2 is better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper argues that pupil size and alpha power are multifaceted, modality-dependent indices of cognitive demand, not interchangeable measures. Option 1 reports pupil size increasing with difficulty (a standard effort marker) and alpha decreasing with visual difficulty (the classic alpha-desynchronization-with-load pattern), plus a negative pupil-alpha trial correlation. Option 2 reverses these: pupil decreasing with demand and alpha increasing, with a positive correlation. Option 2's pattern would undermine the conventional account of pupil dilation and alpha as demand/effort indices that the paper engages with, so Option 1 is better news for the paper's framing.

The paper argues that pupil size and alpha power are multifaceted, diverging indices of cognitive demand with modality-dependent dynamics. Option 1 reports pupil size decreasing and alpha increasing with difficulty, plus a positive pupil-alpha correlation. Option 2 reports pupil increasing and alpha decreasing, with a negative correlation. Both preserve the same core claim of divergence and modality dependence. The directional results differ, but the paper's thesis about multifaceted, dissociable indices is supported equally by both. Option 1's pattern (pupil down, alpha up with load) is more in line with commonly reported alpha-inhibition and pupil-effort findings, but the paper itself does not defend a specific direction, so the difference is only modestly favorable.

The paper proposes that VGLUT3 is a vital contributor to HD pathophysiology and a viable therapeutic target. The two versions differ in mechanism details: Option 1 reports activation of Akt/ERK1/2 and short-term memory rescue with no change in microgliosis; Option 2 reports suppression of Akt/ERK1/2, long-term memory rescue, and no change in astrogliosis. Activation of pro-survival Akt/ERK1/2 signaling fits a neuroprotective account of VGLUT3 deletion better than suppression, which would be a less coherent survival mechanism. Option 1's microgliosis readout is also a neuroinflammation measure, while Option 2's astrogliosis is a different cell type; neither clearly favors the proposed hypothesis. Overall Option 1 is modestly better news for the paper's neuroprotection account.

The two abstracts differ in key results: Option 1 reports rescue of long-term memory, suppression of Akt/ERK1/2, and no change in astrogliosis; Option 2 reports rescue of short-term memory, activation of Akt/ERK1/2, and no change in microgliosis. The paper proposes VGLUT3 as a viable HD therapeutic target. Suppression of pro-survival Akt/ERK signaling is hard to reconcile with neuronal rescue, so Option 2's activation is more coherent with the neuroprotective account. Option 1's memory and glial findings are also less specific, making Option 2 modestly stronger for the paper's therapeutic claim.

The paper proposes that inhibitory control deficits in heroin addiction, marked by impaired target sensitivity and hypoactivation in cognitive control regions, contribute to self-control lapses. Option 1 reports lower PFC activity and worse sensitivity, which supports this account. Option 2 reports hyperactivation and higher sensitivity, which would undermine the deficit narrative. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that inhibitory control deficits in heroin addiction, shown by impaired sensitivity and hyperactivation in cognitive control regions, contribute to self-control lapses. Option 1 reports hyperactivations and higher sensitivity, which frames the neurobehavioral deficit as compensatory hyperactivation rather than hypoactivation, departing from the hypoactivation account the introduction cites. Option 2 reports hypoactivation and lower sensitivity, matching the common PFC hypoactivation model of addiction and the paper's framing of deficits. Option 2 is the more coherent support for the paper's deficit-based account, so Option 1 is worse news for it.

The paper proposes that autistic perception involves weakened predictive feedback priors, supporting the feedback-imbalance account. Option 1 (attenuated contour integration responses in autistic children) fits that hypothesis, supporting weaker global/predictive processing. Option 2 (enhanced responses) would contradict the proposed weakened-priors account, so it is worse news for the paper's proposed mechanism.

The paper proposes that autism involves weakened predictive feedback 'priors' reducing global contour integration. Option 2 (attenuated illusory contour responses) fits this account directly, supporting the weakened-priors idea. Option 1 (enhanced responses) would contradict the proposed mechanism's implications, so it is worse news for the paper's account.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: the hippocampus is critical for temporal discounting when outcomes are experienced in the moment, not when hypothetical. The only difference is the direction of the lesion effect on the delay-reward trade-off amplitude. Option 1 reports decreased amplitude, meaning hippocampal lesions reduce sensitivity to delay, with persistent choice of delayed options. That reduced trade-off reflects the impaired discounting the paper argues for, supporting its account that the hippocampus drives experiential temporal discounting. Option 2 reports increased amplitude, which would mean stronger delay sensitivity after lesions, contradicting the claimed impairment pattern. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed account.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: the hippocampus is critical for temporal discounting when outcomes are experienced rather than hypothetical. The only difference is the direction of the delay-reward trade-off change: Option 1 reports increased amplitude, Option 2 reports decreased amplitude alongside persistent choice of the delayed option. Persistent choice of the delayed option despite delay increase reflects reduced sensitivity to delay, which is an impairment consistent with the hippocampus mattering for discounting. Option 1's increased amplitude, while described as impaired, is less coherent with the stated persistent delayed choice and so is weaker support for the paper's account. Option 2 therefore aligns more cleanly with the proposed hypothesis, making Option 1 somewhat worse news for it.

The paper proposes that long-term mAChR activation drives plasticity of a hyperadapting CA3 subpopulation whose phenotype depends on M-current. Option 1 reports that M-channel antagonists or agonist reapplication abolish the hyperadaptation phenotype, which supports the M-current-dependent account of the phenotype and its cholinergic sensitivity. Option 2 reports enhancement instead, which would contradict the proposed M-current mechanism. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper argues that long-term mAChR activation uncovers a plastic subset of CA3 neurons whose hyperadaptation phenotype depends on the M-current. Option 1 says M-channel antagonists and AChR agonist reapplication enhance the hyperadaptation phenotype, which is consistent with an M-current-driven mechanism. Option 2 says these manipulations abolish it, which would also be consistent with M-current dependence but suggests a different direction of modulation. Option 1 fits the paper's framing that the phenotype is characterized by a strong M-current and modulated by cholinergic agents more directly, so it reads as somewhat better support for the proposed account.

The paper proposes a physiological role for presynaptic APP at medial perforant path synapses. Option 1 reports APP deficiency altering excitatory neurotransmission and presynaptic deletion increasing efficacy, which supports a role for APP as a modulator of excitatory transmission. Option 2 reports altered inhibitory neurotransmission and decreased efficacy, which would be a different and less coherent story relative to the excitatory-synapse framing of the study. Option 1 therefore fits the paper's proposed account somewhat better.

The two abstracts differ in two places: Option 1 reports APP deficiency altered inhibitory transmission and that presynaptic APP deletion decreased efficacy; Option 2 reports altered excitatory transmission and increased efficacy. The paper proposes a physiological presynaptic role for APP supporting perforant path transmission. A decrease in efficacy upon APP loss (Option 1) fits a supportive, physiological role for presynaptic APP better than an increase (Option 2), which would suggest APP restrains transmission. Option 1 is therefore somewhat better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper's proposed account is that insula DYN/KOR microcircuitry drives excessive alcohol use. Option 1 reports that DYN deletion blocks escalation and reduces intake, KOR antagonism reduces early intake, and IA reduces excitability while increasing excitatory drive, all consistent with a mechanism promoting alcohol use being engaged and then targetable. Option 2 reports the opposite directions for each finding (DYN deletion increases intake, KOR antagonism increases intake, IA increases excitability and decreases excitatory drive), which would undercut a model where this circuit promotes excessive drinking. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that insula DYN/KOR microcircuitry drives excessive alcohol use. Option 1 shows DYN deletion accelerates escalated drinking, KOR antagonism increases intake, and IA increases excitability and reduces excitatory drive. Option 2 shows the opposite: DYN deletion blocks escalation, KOR antagonism reduces intake, and IA decreases excitability while increasing excitatory drive. Option 2's findings fit a model where the DYN/KOR circuit promotes alcohol intake, so Option 2 is better news for the paper's proposed account. Option 1 therefore is worse news for it.

The paper proposes that predictable natural sequences (NSeqs) of USVs are important and that they are encoded selectively in auditory cortex, with social experience enhancing this selectivity. Option 1 reports higher selectivity for NSeqs over RSeqs in naive females and enhanced selectivity after social experience, which supports the paper's central claim that predictive sequences matter and are plastically encoded. Option 2 reports the opposite, undermining that account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the proposed hypothesis.

The paper proposes that predictive, context-specific natural sequences (NSeqs) matter for neural and behavioral encoding of mouse USVs and that social experience shapes this encoding. Option 1 reports lower selectivity for NSeqs in naive females and diminished NSeqs selectivity after social experience, which weakens the claim that predictable sequences are specially represented and plastic. Option 2 reports higher selectivity for NSeqs and enhanced selectivity after experience, directly supporting the paper's thesis. So Option 2 is better news for the proposed account.

The paper proposes that seizures transiently depress the HCVR and cause hypothermia via impaired serotonergic function, with postictal 5-HT enhancement as a preventive strategy. Option 1 reports this depression (decreased HCVR, hypoventilation, hypothermia, and mortality worsened by PCPA, rescued by fenfluramine), which is consistent with and supports the proposed 5-HT-mediated mechanism and the biomarker/prevention rationale. Option 2 reverses the direction (increased HCVR, hyperventilation, hyperthermia), which would contradict the proposed serotonergic-depression account.

The paper proposes that seizures impair serotonergic function, depressing the HCVR and causing hypoventilation and hypothermia, which drives SUDEP risk, and that enhancing postictal 5-HT tone could prevent death. Option 2 describes a prolonged decrease in HCVR, hypoventilation, hypothermia, and increased mortality with PCPA, and fenfluramine reducing this inhibition, which fits the paper's proposed mechanism and protective strategy. Option 1 reports the opposite (enhanced HCVR, hyperventilation), which contradicts the proposed account and would undermine the 5-HT-impairment rationale. Option 2 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that early-life stress degrades temporal processing fidelity in the auditory system, linking it to cognitive problems. Option 1 reports impaired detection of short gaps with reduced neural responses, which fits the proposed degradation account and supports the hypothesis that ELS harms sensory representations. Option 2 reports impaired detection of long gaps with enhanced neural responses, which is a less coherent and weaker fit with the claimed degradation mechanism. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes that early-life stress degrades temporal processing and that this degradation of sensory fidelity could contribute to cognitive problems. Option 1 reports impaired detection of long gaps with enhanced neural responses to gaps, which fits a story of miscoding and degraded representations (the paper's account of ELS-induced vulnerability). Option 2 reports impaired detection of short gaps with reduced neural responses, which is a more internally coherent degradation story in that reduced responses would plausibly explain reduced detection, but it still supports the same hypothesis of ELS degrading sensory fidelity. Both support the proposed account, but Option 1's mismatch of enhanced responses with impaired behavior is less clearly interpretable as degraded fidelity, so Option 2 is somewhat better news for the paper's account.

Both versions propose that opioid receptor activation modulates PVT activity, but they differ in direction and timing. Option 1 reports suppression of firing and inhibitory transmission plus reduced opioid modulation after chronic morphine, which fits a coherent account of opioid-mediated inhibition and tolerance via desensitization/internalization. Option 2 reports enhancement, with reduced modulation after acute exposure, which is less consistent with the desensitization mechanism the paper invokes (desensitization is typically a chronic-exposure phenomenon). Option 1 is therefore the more internally coherent and plausible finding for the paper's proposed account.

Both abstracts share the same framing: opioid receptors modulate PVT activity, with reduced modulation after morphine exposure via desensitization and internalization. The key difference is direction. Option 1 reports that opioid receptor activation enhances PVT firing and inhibitory transmission, while Option 2 reports suppression. Option 2 also says reduced modulation follows chronic rather than acute exposure. The paper's proposed account is that opioid receptors act on PVT and that receptor desensitization and internalization reduce modulation after morphine. Option 1's enhancement with acute-exposure desensitization is a coherent, specific mechanism; Option 2's suppression with chronic-exposure desensitization is equally coherent. Neither clearly favors the paper's account more, so the balance is near even, with a slight edge to Option 1 for the acute-exposure desensitization framing matching the proposed mechanism more directly.

The paper proposes that paired LAS-TMS induces plasticity, specifically an increase in corticoreticular connection efficacy, and promotes the protocol as a useful new tool. Option 1 reports LTP-like enhancement of TMS responses, which supports the proposed mechanism and the protocol's utility. Option 2 reports LTD-like depression, which would contradict the claimed potentiation of corticoreticular connections and weaken the proposed utility. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's account.

The paper proposes that paired LAS-TMS induces plasticity in corticoreticular connections and presents the protocol as a useful new tool for boosting motor recovery. Option 1 reports LTD (diminished TMS responses), which is a depression of the pathway and runs against the recovery-boosting goal. Option 2 reports LTP (enhanced responses), which would support the protocol's utility for facilitating motor pathways. Option 2 is therefore better news for the paper's proposed account.

The two abstracts are identical in framing and conclusions; they differ only in which SSRI is studied (escitalopram/fluoxetine vs sertraline/paroxetine) and the corresponding numbers, which are the same values assigned to different drugs. The paper's proposed account (compartmentalized SSRI-SERT interactions in membranes/organelles) is supported equally by both versions, so the difference is not good or bad news for the proposed account.

The two abstracts are identical except for the specific drugs studied (sertraline/paroxetine vs escitalopram/fluoxetine) and their reported kinetics and accumulation values. The paper's proposal is that intracellular/membrane-localized SSRI-SERT interactions matter, supported by drug-accumulation and equilibration data. Option 1 reports sertraline with faster equilibration (few s) and paroxetine with 200-300 s, and membrane accumulation of 18-fold and 180-fold; Option 2 reports escitalopram with the same few-s equilibration and fluoxetine with the same 200-300 s, and identical accumulation figures. Since the numbers are mapped identically, the news value for the paper's account is essentially neutral.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: sleep loss shifts brain morphology in an aging-like direction and is reversible by recovery sleep. The only difference is the magnitude of brain-age increase after total sleep deprivation: 1-2 years in Option 1 versus 4-5 years in Option 2. A larger aging-like shift provides stronger support for the paper's proposed account that sleep loss accelerates brain aging, so Option 2 is better news for the hypothesis. Option 1's smaller effect is weaker support, though still consistent with the account.

Both abstracts share the same hypothesis: sleep loss shifts brain morphology in an aging-like direction, reversible by recovery sleep. The only difference is the magnitude of brain-age increase after total sleep deprivation: 4-5 years in Option 1 versus 1-2 years in Option 2. A larger aging-like shift provides stronger support for the paper's proposed account that sleep loss accelerates brain aging, so Option 1 is better news for the paper's thesis.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of vmPFC activation for positive and negative feedback on highly connected traits. Option 1 has positive feedback producing higher vmPFC activation and negative feedback lower, which fits the paper's proposed account that the brain selectively enhances positive feedback and attenuates negative feedback to maintain positivity and coherence. Option 2 reverses this pattern, contradicting the proposed mechanism of constrained, positivity-preserving updating. So Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of vmPFC activation for positive versus negative feedback on highly dependent traits. Option 1 reports that positive feedback yields less vmPFC activation and negative feedback more, which fits the paper's proposed account of selectively attenuating threatening feedback to preserve positivity and coherence. Option 2 reverses this pattern, which would undercut the constrained-updating mechanism the paper defends. So Option 1 is better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes a nutrient-sensitive RL model in which preferred nutrients drive subjective value and learning. Option 1 says monkeys chose preferred nutrients even when associated with lower reward probability, and that recent rewards with preferred nutrients influenced choices more strongly. This supports the nutrient-value account, since preference-driven choice despite lower probability is the signature the model needs. Option 2 reverses both findings (discarding preferred nutrients at higher probability, weaker influence), which undercuts the proposed account. Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes a nutrient-sensitive RL model. Option 1 reports that recent rewards influenced choices less when containing preferred nutrients and that monkeys discarded preferred nutrients despite higher reward probability; Option 2 reports the opposite pattern (stronger influence and choosing preferred nutrients despite lower probability). Option 2's findings are more consistent with nutrient-driven subjective value guiding choice, which is the paper's central claim, so Option 1 is weaker support for the proposed model.

The paper proposes that the self-concept is conceptualized as self-importance and represented in a specific brain region. Option 1 locates this representation in the medial prefrontal cortex, which the abstract frames as the answer to where the self is represented, with clear dissociations from self-descriptiveness and friend's self-importance. Option 2 instead places it in the anterior cingulate cortex with otherwise identical logic, so it is equally supportive of the self-importance account but offers a different localization. Since the paper's central claim is the mPFC-based account and option 1 matches the commonly expected self-referential locus, option 1 is somewhat better news for the proposed hypothesis.

Both versions present the same design and claim that the self-concept is conceptualized as self-importance and represented in a single region. They differ only in the region: ACC in Option 1 versus mPFC in Option 2. The paper's proposed account is that self-importance is the key representational dimension; the choice of region is a secondary detail. Neither option is clearly better news for the paper's central claim, since both support it equally, so the difference is near neutral.

The paper proposes that rehabilitation restores neurovascular coupling and that the superior frontal gyrus is a neuromodulation target, with restoration of executive control and compensation of frontoparietal integration. Option 1 reports reduced CBF-fALFF correlation and increased CBF/fALFF in the superior frontal gyrus (linked to motor gains) with decreased thalamic ratio, which fits a restoration-plus-compensation account. Option 2 reports the opposite direction: enhanced global coupling and decreased superior frontal ratio, which would undercut the proposed executive-control mechanism. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ only in the direction of the reported changes. Option 1 reports enhanced CBF-fALFF correlations and CBF/fALFF increases in the superior frontal gyrus that track motor improvement, supporting the paper's proposed account of rehabilitation restoring executive control and neurovascular coupling. Option 2 reports the opposite directions, which would undercut the proposed dual-mechanism account and the superior frontal gyrus as a target. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper proposes a multimodal MRI-LSM correlation platform and MRI signatures as biomarkers. Option 1 reports quantitative MRI differences between tumor and contralateral hemisphere and model-specific signatures that differ greatly, which supports the utility of MRI metrics as tumor biomarkers that can be decoded and used clinically. Option 2 reports no MRI differences and only slight signature differences, undermining the value of the MRI biomarkers the paper advocates. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's proposed approach.

The paper proposes a correlative MRI-LSM platform and argues that MRI signatures can be derived and used to interpret tumor biomarkers. Option 1 reports no MRI differences between tumor and contralateral hemisphere and only slight model differences, which weakens the premise that MRI signatures are distinctive and informative. Option 2 reports clear tumor-versus-contralateral MRI differences and great between-model differences, which better supports the utility of MRI signatures and the platform's ability to characterize tumors. Option 2 is therefore better news for the proposed approach.

The paper proposes an extended exponential-integrate-and-fire model explaining diverse L1 interneuron firing features via K+ and Ca2+ channels. Option 1 reports irregular firing in VIP cells explained by square-wave bursting and strong adaptation plus slowly inactivating K+ channels, which is the mechanistic account the paper defends and fits its fast-slow analysis. Option 2 reports regular firing instead, which would undercut the proposed mechanism of irregular firing via bursting. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's model.

The two abstracts differ in whether VIP cells and the square-wave bursting mechanism are described as regular or irregular firing, and in naming the late-spiking cell type (Chandelier vs neurogliaform). The paper's proposed account is that VIP cells' firing arises from strong adaptation interacting with a slowly inactivating K+ channel, and that the bursting mechanism explains the firing pattern. Option 1's regular firing is the mechanistically coherent, explained pattern for adaptation-driven VIP firing; Option 2's irregular firing is a less natural fit for an adaptation-plus-slow-K+ explanation. So Option 1 supports the paper's account somewhat better.

The paper proposes that acidification suppresses seizures by reducing excitatory pyramidal neuron firing via NaV1.2 inhibition, with interneurons unaffected. Option 1 matches this mechanism exactly. Option 2 reverses it, claiming interneuron firing is reduced while pyramidal firing is unaffected, which would undermine the proposed account of seizure suppression through reduced excitation. Option 1 is therefore clearly better news for the paper's hypothesis.

Both versions describe the same hypothesis: acidosis suppresses seizures. Option 1 proposes the mechanism that acid reduces interneuron firing via NaV1.2 inhibition, with excitatory neurons unaffected, and interneuron suppression as the seizure-protective basis. Option 2 instead proposes that acid reduces pyramidal (excitatory) firing via NaV1.2, with interneurons unaffected. The paper's own mechanistic story is that NaV1.2 is interneuron-predominant (Option 1 is consistent with that), while Option 2 contradicts the channel-expression logic it invokes. Option 1 is therefore more coherent and better supports the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that C. elegans has multiple new inhibitory ligand-gated channels and a polymodal channel. Option 1 reports choline as the primary ligand for the inhibitory channels, a surprising and specific finding that strengthens the novelty of the ligand-receptor pairs. It also reports aminergic activation of LGC-39, which fits the polymodal claim. Option 2 reports acetylcholine as the primary ligand, which is less novel, and histamine instead of an aminergic ligand, which is a narrower claim. Option 1 therefore reads as stronger support for the proposed diverse repertoire.

Both abstracts report the same discovery of new inhibitory C. elegans channels, differing in ligand identity. Option 1 says the primary ligand is acetylcholine (fitting the paper's framing of inhibitory ACh-gated channels as an understudied class that the study expands), and that LGC-39 responds to cholinergic and histaminic ligands. Option 2 says choline is the primary ligand and that LGC-39 responds to aminergic ligands, which would make the channels less clearly ACh-gated and the polymodal claim less specific. The paper's central thesis is the diversity of ACh-gated inhibitory channels, so Option 1 supports it better.

The two abstracts differ only in whether EE's mitigating effect on RS decline is most pronounced when evidence accumulation rates are shallowest (Option 1) or steepest (Option 2). The paper proposes that EEG evidence accumulation metrics index neurocognitive vulnerability and that cognitive reserve operates in neurophysiological markers. Option 1 makes the reserve effect concentrated in the vulnerable (shallow-slope) group, which fits a story where EE buffers those with the weakest accumulation, supporting the vulnerability-indexing claim. Option 2 would place the benefit in efficient accumulators, which is less obviously a vulnerability story. So Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ only in whether EE's mitigating effect on RS decline is most pronounced when evidence accumulation rates are steepest (Option 1) or shallowest (Option 2). The paper proposes that EEG evidence accumulation metrics index cognitive reserve and neurocognitive vulnerability. A steepest-rate result (Option 1) fits a cleaner, more interpretable pattern where high-efficiency accumulation is where reserve shows, supporting the account of EEG accumulation as a marker of reserve. Shallowest-rate (Option 2) would suggest the reserve effect concentrates in the weakest processing, which is less coherent with the efficiency-based framing. So Option 1 is modestly better news for the paper's proposed account.

Both abstracts share the same framing: synaptic changes support memory, and the paper proposes synapse-specific, state-dependent modulation that may aid consolidation. Option 1 reports coherent, specific, interpretable patterns (wake-up at PP-DG, NREM-up at SC-CA1, REM-down at Fx-NAc, weak modulation at Fx-PFC/Fx-Amy) that fit a synapse-specific consolidation account. Option 2 has garbled, internally inconsistent statements (a bracketed fragment, REM increase at PP-DG/SC-CA1 contradicting the NREM framing, and strong modulation at Fx-PFC/Fx-Amy that conflicts with the correlation pattern), which weakens support for the proposed account. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's hypothesis.

The paper argues that brain-state-dependent, synapse-specific modulation of evoked responses exists and may contribute to memory consolidation. Option 1 reports strong, clear state modulation at multiple pathways (decreases in wake at PP-DG, NREM decreases at SC-CA1, REM changes at Fx-NAc, strong vigilance modulation at Fx-PFC and Fx-Amy), which better supports the claim of rich synapse-specific modulation. Option 2 reports weaker modulation at Fx-PFC and Fx-Amy, undermining the central synapse-specific account somewhat, though it still shows modulation. Option 1 is therefore somewhat better news for the paper's proposed account.

Both options share the same core hypothesis: beta oscillations encode RPE in striatum. They differ only in which striatal division shows stronger RPE representation. Option 1 (ventral/limbic stronger) matches the paper's emphasis on a major ventral striatum contribution to learning updates, a finding that supports the proposed account of RPE-linked beta activity. Option 2 reverses this, emphasizing dorsal striatum, which would weaken the paper's stated ventral-focused conclusion. So Option 1 is clearly better news for the paper's proposed account.

Both options share the same core claim that beta oscillations encode RPE in striatum. They differ only in which striatal territory dominates: Option 1 says dorsal (sensorimotor and associative) stronger than ventral, Option 2 says ventral stronger than dorsal. The paper's proposed account emphasizes beta-band RPE encoding and a contribution of a specific striatal division. Option 1 supports a dorsal-striatum account of learning updates, which aligns with the paper's framing of dorsal contribution as a major finding; Option 2 would undercut that emphasis. Hence Option 1 is somewhat better news for the paper's proposed account.

The paper proposes that chronic ethanol tolerance is a distinct memory-like state molecularly separate from rapid tolerance. Option 1 states chronic tolerance is independent of Hr38/Nr4a and suppressed by Sirt1, while rapid tolerance is enhanced by Sirt1, reinforcing the molecular distinction between forms. Option 2 instead makes chronic tolerance Hr38-dependent and enhanced by Sirt1, which would blur the claimed molecular separation between chronic and rapid tolerance. Option 1 therefore better supports the paper's central account of distinct molecular bases.

The paper proposes that chronic ethanol tolerance is a distinct memory-like state that depends on Hr38/Nr4a and is enhanced by Sirt1. Option 1 reports chronic tolerance dependent on Hr38 and enhanced by Sirt1, which supports the proposed molecular account. Option 2 reports Hr38 independence and Sirt1 suppression, contradicting the proposed model's molecular distinctions. Option 1 is therefore better news for the paper's account.

The two abstracts differ only in the causal ordering of PKCδ with TrkB and DAG. Option 1 states PKCδ is activated downstream of TrkB and DAG production, the conventional pathway placement that fits the paper's proposed model of PKCδ as an effector in plasticity. Option 2 reverses this, stating PKCδ activation leads to TrkB and DAG production, which is biologically less coherent with the paper's framing of PKCδ as a downstream integrator of plasticity signals. Option 1 therefore better supports the paper's proposed account.

The two abstracts differ only in the causal ordering of PKCδ relative to TrkB and DAG. Option 1 says PKCδ activation leads to TrkB and DAG production, placing PKCδ upstream. Option 2 says PKCδ is activated downstream of TrkB and DAG, which fits the canonical signaling model and the paper's dual-role framing.
